what_it_does: A longstanding bottleneck in running AI models on chips is the constant shuttling of data between the processing units and the separate memory chips — the processor finishes a calculation and then has to wait for the next batch of numbers to arrive. Compute-in-memory (CIM) is an approach that puts simple math circuitry directly inside the memory array, so data never has to travel far. CIMFlow is a software-plus-simulation toolkit that helps chip designers use this technique for deep neural network workloads. It provides a compiler (a program that translates a neural network description into specific hardware instructions) and a simulator (a program that models the hardware's behavior) under a single roof. The toolkit also tackles a practical constraint: CIM arrays are physically small, so large neural network layers must be split across many arrays — CIMFlow handles this partitioning automatically. Based on the abstract, the framework appears to fill a gap where previously no unified end-to-end tool existed for digital CIM design.
